title: Probe: multiplex windowing latency scratchpad
content:
Goal:
- Quick exploration of small-window multiplexing (coalescing short concurrent requests into short 'multiplex windows') and its effect on tail latency and KV cache reuse for short prompt workloads.

Motivation / context:
- Many interactive features send lots of tiny requests (8-40 token prompts).
- Continuous batching is great but we also saw cases where small batching causes p99 regressions because of head-of-line blocking or extra scheduling hops.
- Idea: open short multiplex window (1-50ms) at ingress to merge requests to same model shard and reuse warmed KV slots without invoking full batch rebuilds.

Hypothesis:
- Small windows (1-5ms) should increase throughput and reduce average cost with minimal p99 impact for steady load.
- Larger windows (20-50ms) increase p99 significantly due to queuing; but may improve efficiency under high burstiness.

Experiment setup:
- Hardware: single A100-80GB instance (dev pool), 16 worker threads, GPU pinned.
- Model: redwood-small-v2 (fp16) + quantized variant for one run.
- Workload: synthetic clients (100 clients) issuing 10-40 token prompts. 2 arrival patterns: Poisson (lambda tuned) and microburst (packets of 200 reqs in 30ms every 2s).
- Window sizes tested: 0ms (baseline, no multiplex), 1ms, 5ms, 20ms, 50ms.
- Measurement windows: 10 minutes steady run per config. Warm-up 2 minutes discarded.
- Metrics: q50/q95/q99 latency (server-side from ingress->first-token), p99 token-rate, KV-cache hit ratio, throughput (qps), CPU worker stall % (from perf counters).

Raw summary table (representative, Poisson):

window_ms | qps  | kv_hit% | p50_ms | p95_ms | p99_ms | worker_stall%
--------- | ---- | ------- | ------ | ------ | ------ | -----------
0         | 840  | 12      | 18     | 72     | 145    | 7.2
1         | 920  | 21      | 17     | 69     | 152    | 8.1
5         | 980  | 35      | 16     | 68     | 160    | 10.5
20        | 1020 | 58      | 19     | 92     | 260    | 22.4
50        | 1050 | 67      | 25     | 140    | 480    | 41.0

Observations (Poisson):
- qps increases monotonically with window size (more coalescing).
- KV hit% rises significantly at 5-20ms — suggests windows let short-lived KV contexts be reused across coalesced requests.
- Tail latency (p99) modestly worse at 1-5ms vs baseline, but explodes at 20ms+ (queueing dominates).
- Worker stall increases with window size, indicating increased waiting inside scheduler for window closure.

Microburst pattern results (high instantaneous load):
- Baseline (0ms): severe p95/p99 spikes, frequent GPU oversubscribe events, drop/retry behavior.
- 5ms window: substantial smoothing of bursts, p95 improved, p99 similar to baseline under this pattern.
- 20-50ms: better amortization, but many requests experience added queuing latency; user-visible tail likely unacceptable.

Notes on quantized variant:
- Quantized model had slightly higher single-request overhead (token fusion cost) but benefited more from multiplex windows (KV hit delta larger). p50 similar, p99 increases follow same trend.

Micro-observations / traces:
- Traces show many 'mini-batches' formed inside windows where KV cache reuse avoided full attention recompute for prefix tokens.
- When window aligns with existing warm KV (cache primed), p50 drops by ~3ms vs baseline.
- If window closes after GPU dispatch delay -> some requests hit additional scheduling hop (adds ~8-12ms). This correlates with worker_stall% > 20%.

Quick conclusions:
- Micro-windowing (1-5ms) is a promising sweet spot: measurable qps and cost benefits, small p99 risk under Poisson; helps with moderate bursts.
- Larger windows (20ms+) are only useful for heavy-bursty ingress where throughput-cost tradeoff outweighs added queuing latency. Not safe as default for interactive SLOs.
- Quantized models amplify the efficiency gains, so windows are higher ROI when using smaller (quant) model variants.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Re-run on multi-shard setup (N=4) — inter-shard coalescing behavior unknown.
- Try dynamic windowing: start 1ms, expand to 10ms if detected burstiness > X qps for Y ms. Simulate with adaptive policy.
- Add client-side latency budget enforcement: if client is latency-sensitive, bypass windows via header flag.
- Evaluate effect with streaming-first-token timeline (when first-token latency is critical).
- Investigate fairness/priority interaction: high-priority lanes should opt out of waiting windows.

Suggested next steps:
- Prototype dynamic-window controller in the scheduler (PR link above).
- Add per-tenant opt-in flag and metrics dashboard: window_ms, coalesced_batch_size, kv_hit_rate, window_wait_ms histogram.
- Run overnight sweep across fleet-size emulation (4x shards) and record p99 changes.

Notes to self (quick):
- When writing PR: include microburst traces and the ascii table above.
- Keep default window disabled for hosted api until dynamic policy and priority lanes exist.
- Low-risk starter: enable 1ms window in internal dev pool; watch p99 alerting for 48h.

Misc raw log excerpt (example trace lines, redacted ids):
- [2025-11-20T14:03:12Z] ingress: req A arrive, window open(1ms), coalesced->batch 4, gpu_dispatched at +1.9ms, first_token at +18.2ms
- [2025-11-20T14:03:12Z] ingress: req B arrive, same window, kv_hit true, first_token +15.8ms
- [2025-11-20T14:07:05Z] burst start: 220 reqs / 30ms, baseline p99 520ms, 5ms-window p99 172ms

Scratch rough code sketch for adaptive window heuristic:
- monitor short-term arrival rate r(t) over 100ms sliding window
- if r(t) > threshold_high -> increase window to min(max_window, current*2)
- if r(t) < threshold_low -> decay window back to default (1ms)
- constraints: do not exceed per-tenant max_wait_ms SLA header

End notes: keep this as personal sandbox doc. Will distill into engineer-facing writeup after multi-shard validation.
